edition.deck: France faces questions over the scale of unrest as conflict, political tensions and fresh investigations shape the day’s news.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritised significant developments and reporting with a fresh angle. Where reports give different figures or leave responsibility unresolved, the copy preserves those distinctions rather than treating them as settled.

content.headline: France confronts the aftermath of widespread riots and looting
content.shortHeadline: France confronts the aftermath of widespread riots
content.standfirst: After demonstrations over living costs, schools and public services, masked groups looted shops and set fires in cities across France. Officials and politicians now face questions over the policing and causes of the violence.

image.caption: Limoges town hall burns after an apparent arson attack during the protests.

sources.originalTitle: French government in crisis talks after ‘colossal failure of the state’
Burnt out cars and shattered glass on Paris streets after protests turn to riots and looting
'Blame game' efter demonstrationer i Frankrig: Korrespondent spår en politisk diskussion, der vil vare til præsidentvalget

segments.body: France was left counting the cost of a day of demonstrations and disorder, with shops looted and public buildings and vehicles set alight. Peaceful marches over schools, public services and living costs took place alongside separate groups who clashed with police and caused damage. The Guardian reported more than 2,000 arrests; the BBC reported about 1,800.

segments.title: Questions over the response
segments.body: Mayors and opposition figures criticised the authorities’ preparation and policing, while the government blamed far-left groups and criminals. DR correspondent Stéphanie Surrugue said the scale of the crowds exceeded police expectations and predicted a continuing political dispute over who was responsible, potentially lasting through the presidential campaign.

perspectives.body: DR’s correspondent focuses on the gap between expected and reported turnout, and the questions this raises about police intelligence and deployment. She warns that arguments over responsibility could overshadow protesters’ demands.

content.headline: European diplomats attacked by settlers in the West Bank; Israel investigates
content.shortHeadline: European diplomats attacked in the West Bank
content.standfirst: A European delegation visiting Taybeh to assess settler attacks on Palestinians was confronted by masked settlers, according to reports. Israeli officials condemned the violence, while Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said the sequence and individual responsibility remain under investigation.

image.caption: Masked settlers are accused of confronting the European delegation’s convoy.

sources.originalTitle: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank

segments.body: The delegation, including officials from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church, was visiting the occupied West Bank village of Taybeh. Video showed masked settlers confronting its convoy; reports said stones were thrown. Belgium said a consular car’s window was smashed, and French mayor Bernard Baudoux said he was kicked and beaten with iron bars.

segments.title: Condemnation and disputed details
segments.body: Belgium, France, Poland and the EU called for accountability. Israel’s military condemned the violence and said it was investigating, while Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said the visit had not been coordinated with the army. Netanyahu’s office urged caution, saying social-media images did not establish the full sequence or who was responsible.

content.headline: Ukraine and Russia trade major strikes as energy ceasefire collapses
content.shortHeadline: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as energy truce collapses
content.standfirst: A Ukrainian drone attack hit oil and technology sites in St Petersburg, while Russian strikes killed a woman in Zaporizhzhia, according to local officials. The exchanges underline the collapse of a proposed energy truce as winter approaches.

image.caption: Smoke rises from the St Petersburg oil terminal after a reported Ukrainian drone strike.

sources.originalTitle: Two killed and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine trade blows on power infrastructure
Oil facilities hit in deadly overnight attack on St Petersburg
Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies

segments.body: Ukraine launched a large drone attack on Russian targets, including an oil terminal, an oil depot, warehouses and data centres in St Petersburg, according to the Guardian. Russian authorities said more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones were downed across the country; the reported numbers and damage are claims from officials and companies. A separate Russian attack in Zaporizhzhia killed a woman and injured at least two people, local officials said.

segments.title: Energy infrastructure under pressure
segments.body: The attacks followed the breakdown of a proposed “energy ceasefire” announced by Donald Trump. Ukraine says Russian attacks on its energy sector continued; President Volodymyr Zelensky said energy sites in four regions were hit in one night and families remained without power. Trump has also paused sanctions legislation against Russia, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio describing the suspension as a 60-day period to assess its economic impact.

content.headline: Six ships attacked in 10 days as Black Sea shipping risks rise
content.shortHeadline: A surge in Black Sea ship attacks raises risks to crews and trade
content.standfirst: A series of attacks on commercial vessels has brought the maritime conflict closer to NATO countries’ shores. Responsibility for individual strikes is not conclusively established, while insurers and regional officials warn of growing danger to shipping and trade.

image.caption: The chemical tanker Wine Trader was attacked near Romania’s coast, according to the report.

sources.originalTitle: Intensifying drone attacks on ships in Black Sea bring war ever closer to Nato shores

segments.body: Six ships were attacked in 10 days in the Black Sea, according to the Guardian’s account, with sailors killed and others missing. The attacks have reached waters near Bulgaria and Romania. A maritime risk analyst cited in the report says attacks have increased since July and estimates Russian forces are responsible for most of them; the report also notes that officials say they lack clear, conclusive evidence to assign responsibility in specific cases.

segments.title: Risks beyond the crews
segments.body: Shipping operators have become more reluctant to use the route and insurance costs have risen, the report says. Analysts warn that disruption could affect grain and other exports. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev called attacks near his country’s waters unacceptable but said there was no conclusive evidence identifying either side as responsible for the incidents.

content.headline: Alberta votes on whether to start a legal path to separation
content.shortHeadline: Alberta votes on whether to begin a separation referendum process
content.standfirst: Voters in the oil-rich Canadian province are being asked whether to remain in Canada or begin the legal process for a future binding independence referendum. A “yes” would not itself make Alberta independent.

image.caption: Albertans are voting on whether to begin the process for a future separation referendum.

sources.originalTitle: Why is Alberta voting to separate from Canada, and how likely is it to happen?

segments.body: The question on Monday’s ballot is whether Alberta should remain a Canadian province or start the legal process required to hold a later binding referendum on separation. Premier Danielle Smith supports remaining in Canada but says she will accept the result. The vote is a first step in a process, not a direct vote on independence.

segments.title: A divided debate
segments.body: Supporters of separation cite disputes over federal control, environmental policy and the province’s contribution to Canada. First Nations have criticised the referendum plan after a court ruled that an earlier citizen-led petition did not adequately consult Indigenous communities. Polls cited by the BBC indicate most Albertans favour staying in Canada, though the question has galvanised a political debate about the province’s future.

content.headline: Synthetic drugs deepen the US overdose crisis as supplies become harder to know
content.shortHeadline: Synthetic drugs deepen America’s overdose crisis
content.standfirst: A BBC investigation in Ohio and Illinois finds drugs increasingly mixed with synthetic opioids and animal tranquilizers, making their effects less predictable. Recovery workers say people can overdose without knowing what they have taken.

image.caption: The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers during an early-morning search at Cook County jail.

sources.originalTitle: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis

segments.body: In Columbus, drug testing found medetomidine in a sample brought in by a man who thought he was using fentanyl. The BBC reports that synthetic tranquilizers such as medetomidine and xylazine may be mixed with opioids or stimulants. Naloxone can reverse opioid overdoses but does not counteract these tranquilizers, according to the report.

segments.title: A changing supply
segments.body: Recovery workers and a county sheriff described drug supplies that are increasingly unpredictable, including stimulants contaminated with fentanyl and synthetic cannabinoids brought into a jail on paper. US overdose deaths fell from about 110,000 at their 2022 peak to around 70,000 last year, the BBC reports, but the investigation cautions that the crisis has changed rather than ended.

content.headline: Amelia Earhart plane search resumes after weather delay, with no evidence yet
content.shortHeadline: Earhart plane search resumes after three-day weather delay
content.standfirst: Researchers have returned to Nikumaroro in Kiribati to investigate an underwater object that may be aircraft wreckage. The team has not reported finding evidence of Earhart’s plane, and the object’s identity remains disputed.

image.caption: Expedition member Sirisha Bandla, right, said the crew was excited to return to Nikumaroro.

sources.originalTitle: Search for Amelia Earhart's plane resumes after stormy weather

segments.body: An expedition searching for Amelia Earhart’s aircraft has resumed after rough seas and strong winds kept the team aboard its vessel for three days. Researchers are investigating the so-called Taraia Object, seen in aerial images in the lagoon at Nikumaroro, but have yet to report promising evidence that it is the missing plane.

segments.title: A theory still unproven
segments.body: Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared in 1937 while trying to reach Howland Island. One theory is that they reached Nikumaroro and that Earhart died there as a castaway. Some explorers doubt that the Taraia Object is aircraft wreckage, and previous searches for Earhart’s plane have not confirmed a discovery.

content.headline: Gabon moves to protect iboga as interest in its potential drug grows
content.shortHeadline: Gabon moves to protect iboga as overseas drug interest grows
content.standfirst: A draft export ban and new benefit-sharing rules aim to protect the plant and Gabonese cultural knowledge as overseas interest in ibogaine rises. Evidence for possible medical uses is still preliminary, and overharvesting is already a concern.

image.caption: Participants take part in a Bwiti ceremony involving iboga root bark.

sources.originalTitle: The next ayahuasca? Gabon fights to protect sacred plant from US drug companies

segments.body: Gabon’s government adopted a draft decree in September that would prohibit exports of iboga and its derivatives. A May decree recognised traditional knowledge associated with the plant as national heritage and requires benefit-sharing for commercial use. Practitioners say iboga is part of Bwiti traditions, not simply a raw material for drug development.

segments.title: Promise, uncertainty and conservation
segments.body: Researchers have reported early findings on ibogaine as a possible treatment for addiction and other conditions, but the report stresses that a small, uncontrolled study cannot establish efficacy. Conservationists warn that harvesting whole roots can kill the slow-growing plant; one former environment minister described wild iboga as rare and poorly studied. Gabon’s challenge is to protect both the species and the knowledge associated with it.

content.headline: Reform activist suspended after undercover remarks about Muslims and asylum
content.shortHeadline: Reform suspends activist over remarks about Muslims and asylum seekers
content.standfirst: An undercover ITV investigation recorded Jason Powell saying Muslims could not be British and advocating concentration camps for people arriving by small boat. Reform suspended him as questions grow over its candidate vetting and response to racism.

sources.originalTitle: Aspiring Reform MP who said ‘you cannot be Muslim and British’ suspended
Reform candidate filmed saying asylum seekers should be put in ‘concentration camps’

segments.body: Reform UK suspended activist Jason Powell after ITV recorded him saying “you cannot be a Muslim and British” and advocating concentration camps for people crossing the Channel. The investigation also recorded two elected Reform councillors discussing executions of grooming-gang suspects. The councillors were not, at the time of the report, under investigation by the party.

segments.title: Questions over the party’s response
segments.body: The Muslim Council of Britain said suspensions alone do not address what it described as a culture of hatred within Reform. The party said it had improved its vetting and would investigate members who behaved inappropriately; Nigel Farage has argued that parties cannot vet people for comments they make in the future.

content.headline: Manchester committee to investigate £55m loans to City owner-linked firms
content.shortHeadline: Manchester committee to examine £55m loans to City owner-linked firms
content.standfirst: A Greater Manchester scrutiny committee is to examine public loans made to companies controlled by Manchester City’s Abu Dhabi owner while Andy Burnham was mayor. The authority says the loans have been repaid and defends the fund’s wider housing record.

image.caption: Andy Burnham and Manchester City chairman Khaldoon al-Mubarak at the Etihad Stadium in 2019.

sources.originalTitle: Manchester City owner’s £55m housing loan while Burnham was mayor investigated
The mystery Man City dinner that raises awkward questions for PM over £55m loans

segments.body: Greater Manchester’s overview and scrutiny committee plans to investigate loans totalling £55m to three companies ultimately controlled by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan. The funding, issued in 2017 through a housing investment fund, supported the Manchester Life development. The combined authority says the loans have been repaid in full.

segments.title: Questions about transparency
segments.body: The investigation follows reporting that Burnham attended hospitality at Manchester City weeks before loans were approved, and that records of meetings later disappeared from the authority’s website. A councillor leading the review said the fund’s approval process had been criticised as opaque. The authority says lending decisions were made publicly and that the fund helped build homes without cost to taxpayers.

content.headline: NHS assessment warns new ward rules could harm trans patients
content.shortHeadline: NHS assessment warns new ward rules may harm trans patients
content.standfirst: An internal impact assessment says NHS England’s new guidance on single-sex wards could cause delays, distress or discrimination for trans patients. It also notes potential benefits for other groups and says clinical need should be prioritised.

sources.originalTitle: New NHS England policy for trans people could have ‘a number of adverse impacts’, report finds

segments.body: NHS England’s new guidance says single-sex wards, toilets and changing rooms should be used according to biological sex. An internal impact assessment reported by the Guardian warns that some trans patients could face delays, be placed in side rooms or avoid seeking care because they fear being outed or discriminated against.

segments.title: Risks and safeguards
segments.body: The assessment also identifies potential benefits for women who are pregnant or breastfeeding and for people with particular religious beliefs. It says clinical need should take priority, that the guidance does not apply in A&E or intensive care, and that the policy should not result in corridor care. NHS England declined to comment to the Guardian.

content.headline: Childcare costs can leave some parents worse off when they work
content.shortHeadline: Childcare funding can leave some parents worse off at work
content.standfirst: Parents on universal credit say they struggle with upfront nursery bills and delayed reimbursements, while support can fall when earnings rise. Researchers recommend replacing the current arrangements with a single scheme.

image.caption: Research found that some parents using universal credit childcare support struggle to work extra hours.

sources.originalTitle: The parents ‘better off’ on universal credit due to childcare trap

segments.body: Universal credit can reimburse 85% of eligible childcare costs, but parents must pay first. If earnings rise enough to end UC eligibility, support may shift to tax-free childcare, which covers 20% of costs up to a yearly limit. Research cited by the i Paper found that 46% of parents using UC childcare support said it did not enable them to work extra hours.

segments.title: A call to simplify support
segments.body: Parents in the research described borrowing to cover fees and waiting months for reimbursements; 49% said the support had not helped reduce their debt. Researchers propose one scheme that removes upfront payments and gradually reduces support as income rises. The Department for Work and Pensions said it had taken steps to help with upfront costs and remained committed to childcare support.

content.headline: Reform mayor under police investigation over alleged sexual images at work
content.shortHeadline: Police investigate Reform mayor over alleged images shown to colleague
content.standfirst: Humberside police are investigating allegations that Hull and East Yorkshire mayor Luke Campbell showed a female colleague naked and sexualised images. Campbell denies the allegations through Reform; he has not been arrested, according to the report.

image.caption: Luke Campbell, right, with Reform UK leader Nigel Farage in 2025.

sources.originalTitle: Police investigate Reform mayor for allegedly sharing ‘naked and sexualised’ images of himself

segments.body: A female colleague said Campbell showed her four naked and sexualised images at work and that she felt shocked and humiliated. She said her offer of a permanent role was later withdrawn. Campbell was questioned under caution earlier this month, the Guardian reported; he has not been arrested in relation to the allegations.

segments.title: Allegations and response
segments.body: Reform said Campbell firmly denies the allegations and described them as coming from a disgruntled employee in a workplace dispute. Witness statements submitted during an internal grievance process are cited in the report. The combined authority said its complaints processes must be conducted fairly and independently.

content.headline: Government-backed low-interest loans for home energy upgrades expected soon
content.shortHeadline: Low-interest loans for heat pumps and solar expected soon
content.standfirst: A government-backed scheme is expected to offer cheaper borrowing for heat pumps, solar panels and batteries, but not insulation. Energy advisers welcome the help for borrowers while warning that families unable to take on debt may be left out.

image.caption: A heat pump, one of the home energy upgrades the proposed loans would cover.

sources.originalTitle: Zero-interest loans for heat pumps set to launch within weeks

segments.body: The proposed Warm Homes Loan Scheme would support loans for heat pumps, solar panels and batteries, with government funding intended to lower lenders’ interest rates. The i Paper reports that the scheme is expected after the Budget at the end of October; the government has not yet announced the full lender list or details.

segments.title: Who may miss out
segments.body: The loans would not cover insulation, which may help heat pumps work more efficiently. Citizens Advice said the scheme could help households able to borrow but warned that families with too much income for means-tested grants and too little disposable income for new debt could be excluded. Possible cuts to the Boiler Upgrade Scheme are under consideration, the report says, but have not been confirmed.

content.headline: Labour faces internal resistance to Andy Burnham’s electoral reform plan
content.shortHeadline: Labour split over Burnham’s plan to change the voting system
content.standfirst: Labour figures warn that proportional representation could weaken constituency links and give smaller parties leverage, while supporters argue an independent commission should examine alternatives. The divide could shape the government’s next manifesto.

image.caption: Andy Burnham has proposed a commission on electoral reform and a manifesto commitment to change the voting system.

sources.originalTitle: Blunkett leads Labour backlash against Burnham’s voting reform

segments.body: Andy Burnham’s proposal for an electoral reform commission and a manifesto commitment to change the voting system has met resistance within Labour. Former home secretary David Blunkett warned that proportional representation could give small parties disproportionate influence; several MPs cited concerns about constituency representation and coalition politics.

segments.title: Supporters call for a review
segments.body: Labour MP Alex Sobel says an independent commission should first assess whether the current first-past-the-post system is fit for purpose, then consider alternatives. He argues that proportional systems can retain a constituency link and says there is support for a commission among Labour MPs and members.

content.headline: Green leader Zack Polanski defends party’s Zionism motion
content.shortHeadline: Polanski defends Green Party motion on Zionism
content.standfirst: Zack Polanski said Zionism is racist “in the practical application of it” and rejected calls to overturn a party motion. His remarks deepen a dispute within the Greens over the wording and its implications.

image.caption: Green Party leader Zack Polanski spoke to the BBC about the party’s motion on Zionism.

sources.originalTitle: Zack Polanski says application of Zionism is racist and no state has right to exist

segments.body: In a BBC interview reported by the Guardian, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said Zionism was racist “in the practical application of it” and described the party’s conference motion as not controversial. Asked about Israel’s right to exist, he said no state has a right to exist under international law.

segments.title: Fallout within the party
segments.body: Polanski said he was not sorry about his handling of the issue and that he agreed with the motion’s broad thrust, while calling debate about terminology unhelpful. The report describes criticism from some Jewish Green members and a difficult period for his leadership after the party conference vote.

content.headline: Danish newspaper editors to complain after photographers say police hit them
content.shortHeadline: Editors to complain after photographers say police hit them
content.standfirst: Photographers from Ekstra Bladet and Politiken say they were struck while covering demonstrations in Copenhagen. The outlets plan complaints; police confirmed officers used batons but said they were still reviewing what happened.

image.caption: Editors at Politiken and Ekstra Bladet plan complaints over the reported treatment of press photographers at a Copenhagen demonstration.

sources.originalTitle: Pressefotografer blev slået under demo - chefredaktør vil anmelde sagen

segments.body: Two photographers covering demonstrations in Copenhagen said police struck them on Saturday. Ekstra Bladet photographer Anthon Unger said he was wearing press identification when he was hit on the arm with a baton. Politiken photographer Thomas Borberg said his camera was smashed and he went to hospital.

segments.title: Police review and planned complaints
segments.body: Politiken’s editor-in-chief said he would complain to Copenhagen Police and report the case to the Independent Police Complaints Authority; Ekstra Bladet’s editor also plans to complain. Police confirmed that uniformed and plainclothes officers had used batons, but did not confirm or deny that the photographers were struck, saying they needed to review their own documentation.

content.headline: Danish electric-car shift avoided nearly DKK 2bn in oil imports, thinktank says
content.shortHeadline: Electric cars avoided nearly DKK 2bn in Danish oil imports, study says
content.standfirst: Thinktank Ember estimates that Denmark’s shift to electric cars since the Iran war began has cut oil imports by the equivalent of about DKK 2bn. The savings mainly benefit drivers, while the state collects less tax than it would from fossil-fuel cars.

image.caption: Electric-car charging points at a dealership in Gladsaxe.

sources.originalTitle: Tænketank: Danske elbiler har sparet os oliekøb for 2 milliarder kroner under Iran-krigen

segments.body: Since the Iran war began on 28 February, Denmark’s electric-car fleet has grown enough to avoid oil imports worth nearly DKK 2bn, according to new figures from energy thinktank Ember. The estimate equates the increase in electric cars over six months to about 13% of Denmark’s 2025 oil imports.

segments.title: Benefits and trade-offs
segments.body: Transport economist Mogens Fosgerau said the savings mainly accrue to car owners, while the state misses out on revenue because electric cars are taxed differently from petrol and diesel vehicles. Ember’s figures put Denmark well above the EU average in reducing oil dependence per person.

content.headline: Denmark’s oldest person confirms she was once a member of the Nazi party
content.shortHeadline: Denmark’s oldest person confirms wartime Nazi party membership
content.standfirst: Kirsten Schwalbe, 112, says she joined DNSAP during the German occupation after her husband asked her to. Historians caution that the membership record alone does not show how long she belonged or whether she was active.

image.caption: Kirsten Schwalbe, who has confirmed that she was listed as a DNSAP member during the occupation.

sources.originalTitle: Danmarks længstlevende var medlem af dansk nazistparti

segments.body: Kirsten Schwalbe, described as the longest-lived Dane on record, has confirmed she was listed as a member of the Danish National Socialist Workers’ Party, DNSAP, during the German occupation. She told TV Midtvest she was not interested in politics and joined after her husband asked her to.

segments.title: What the record establishes
segments.body: Two historians independently confirmed that her name appears in the Bovrup register, although her surname is misspelled there. Historian Charlie Krautwald cautioned that the register records membership but does not establish why someone joined, how long they remained a member or whether they were active. Her publisher said it had not previously known this part of her history.

content.headline: Danish homeowner disputes a DKK 230,000 water bill after meter error
content.shortHeadline: Homeowner disputes DKK 230,000 water bill after meter error
content.standfirst: A homeowner says a bill for almost DKK 250,000 reflects implausible use at a house he rarely visits. The utility says the meter’s confirmed fault has already been credited and that customers are responsible for plumbing on their property.

sources.originalTitle: Boligejer fik pludselig ekstraregning på 230.000 kroner for vand

segments.body: Kim Hansen received a large bill after a meter check indicated he had used about 2,890 cubic metres of water over nine years at a house he used only occasionally. He says he had read the old meter as a decimal figure. A new meter recorded only about 1.5 cubic metres in the first half of this year.

segments.title: The dispute remains unresolved
segments.body: The meter was found to have a 5.4% error, above the permitted 4%, and Hansen received a credit of DKK 13,590. A building expert said the recorded consumption was unusually high for one person but noted that a faulty toilet or pipe could account for heavy use. The utility says the meter was tested at an accredited laboratory and customers are responsible for leaks inside their property.

content.headline: Enhedslisten proposes DKK 50,000 grants for some rural electric-car buyers
content.shortHeadline: Enhedslisten proposes DKK 50,000 grants for rural electric-car buyers
content.standfirst: The party wants to help lower-income rural households replace petrol or diesel cars with electric vehicles, at a proposed cost of DKK 2.5bn for 50,000 households. Eligibility rules and other details have not yet been settled.

image.caption: Enhedslisten proposes help for lower-income rural families who switch to electric cars.

sources.originalTitle: Enhedslisten foreslår tilskud på 50.000 kroner til elbiler

segments.body: Enhedslisten proposes grants of DKK 50,000 for lower-income households in rural areas that replace a petrol or diesel car with an electric vehicle. Political spokesperson Pelle Dragsted says the proposal is intended to help families who need a car but cannot afford an electric one.

segments.title: Proposal ahead of budget talks
segments.body: The party estimates the scheme would support 50,000 households and cost DKK 2.5bn, funded in part by a new corporate tax. The precise eligibility rules are not finalised; the proposal refers to income limits, location and having owned a fossil-fuel car for at least a year. The party presented it ahead of budget negotiations.

content.headline: Family circus closes after 32 years as Denmark’s traditional circuses decline
content.shortHeadline: Cirkus Mascot ends 32 years on the road
content.standfirst: Cirkus Mascot is giving its final performance in Roslev after 32 years. Its director cites age, declining audiences and the demands of running a small circus; six traditional circuses will remain in Denmark.

image.caption: The family-owned Cirkus Mascot has performed 33 seasons before its final show.

sources.originalTitle: I dag har Cirkus Mascot sidste forestilling: 'Det bliver virkelig hårdt'

segments.body: The family-run Cirkus Mascot is closing after its final performance in Roslev. Director Marianne Deleuran said her son wanted to try something else and that the physical work had become harder as she approaches 64. The circus, founded in 1994, moved from touring under a big top to performing in sports halls after the pandemic.

segments.title: A difficult business
segments.body: Deleuran said fewer children attend because they watch more online. The Cirkus Museum’s Mikkel Knudsen also cited bureaucracy, including permits for tents and posters, and difficulties finding workers. He said the industry was in a downturn but remained optimistic about its ability to adapt. Six traditional circuses will remain in Denmark.

content.headline: Hundreds of men’s groups form across Denmark to address loneliness
content.shortHeadline: Hundreds of men’s groups form across Denmark
content.standfirst: Organisations report hundreds of new men’s groups, including workshops, cooking groups and walking clubs. Researchers say the activities can help men build relationships and reduce loneliness, particularly after leaving work.

image.caption: Members of the Green Men’s Community in Hanstholm, one of hundreds of groups reported to have formed in recent years.

sources.originalTitle: Fællesskaber for mænd skyder op i hobetal: Det er godt mod ensomhed
Er du ensom, mand? Her er 4 gode råd til at starte et mandefællesskab

segments.body: Forum for Men’s Health has registered more than 360 men’s groups around Denmark, while Ældre Sagen says its number of groups has tripled in five years. Activities include workshops, cooking and walking. A researcher told DR that shared tasks can make it easier for participants to talk and form relationships.

segments.title: A need that remains
segments.body: Researchers and organisers say groups can be especially valuable when men retire or face changes in family life. Organisers say some groups already have waiting lists and cannot meet demand. The report also notes that men are less likely than women to use some support services despite higher rates of suicide.

content.headline: Vestervig marks 20 years of work to clear derelict houses
content.shortHeadline: Vestervig marks 20 years of work against derelict homes
content.standfirst: A local initiative says it has demolished 29 derelict houses and helped renovate others over two decades. The town’s population has fallen, but organisers point to more children at the school and new families as signs of progress.

sources.originalTitle: 29 spøgelseshuse revet ned i landsby

segments.body: Vestervig Byfornyelse was formed in 2006 to tackle abandoned and deteriorating homes in the town. Since then, 29 houses have been demolished, while others were bought, renovated and sold or rented. The group says it has worked with local volunteers and support from municipal and state funds.

segments.title: Renewal beyond demolition
segments.body: Vestervig has lost 20% of its population over the period, but the group’s deputy chair says school numbers are rising and families are moving in. The initiative has also helped bring two doctors to the town, who will work in former school premises. Organisers expect the work to continue.

content.headline: How Fontaines D.C. built a path from Dublin dive bars to stadiums
content.shortHeadline: Fontaines D.C.’s road from Dublin clubs to stadiums
content.standfirst: The Irish band’s ascent has come through ambitious records, relentless touring and champions on radio and in the industry—not a campaign built around viral moments. Their fifth album arrives as they prepare for a bigger stage.

image.caption: Fontaines D.C., with frontman Grian Chatten at the centre.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The mainstream has come to them’: how did Fontaines DC go from Dublin dive bars to headlining stadiums?

segments.body: Fontaines D.C. formed in Dublin in 2014 and built their following through small venues, steady songwriting and extensive touring. Their first album, Dogrel, reached the UK and Irish top 10 in 2019; now they are heading towards UK stadiums, US arenas and major festival slots, with a fifth album, Dopamine Chamber, arriving alongside that expansion.

segments.title: A less-is-more ascent
segments.body: People around the band point to early support from BBC Radio 6 Music, the label’s emphasis on authenticity and lyrics, and the decision to keep releasing music during lockdown. Music-industry observers also describe the band’s online following as organic rather than manufactured. The story’s contributors see no single explanation for the scale of the rise: talent, commitment, support and luck all played a part.

content.headline: Shygirl’s new album turns a love story toward rock and vulnerability
content.shortHeadline: Shygirl moves from club sounds to rock on Swallow!
content.standfirst: The London artist’s forthcoming album draws on a settled relationship and a new musical direction. She also reflects on the work behind her rise and the barriers she sees for women in the industry.

image.caption: Shygirl in 2026.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I need to prove my family’s sacrifice was worth it’: how pop auteur Shygirl slogged her way to the top

segments.body: Shygirl’s second album, Swallow!, moves away from the hyperpop, UK garage and electronic sounds of her earlier work towards an expansive, guitar-led rock record. She describes it as a response to intimacy and devotion, drawing on her relationship with actor George Smale and a new willingness to let vulnerability shape the songs.

segments.title: Ambition on her own terms
segments.body: Born Blane Muise, Shygirl describes growing up in south-east London with parents who worked a succession of jobs, and says their sacrifices drive her determination. After building a career from club music and leaving a secure day job, she has opened arenas for Beyoncé and Charli xcx. She says gender remains a significant barrier and wants to work with people who challenge the status quo.

content.headline: Fontaines D.C.’s Dopamine Chamber makes stadium rock feel unsettling
content.shortHeadline: Fontaines D.C. turn stadium rock dark on Dopamine Chamber
content.standfirst: The band’s fifth album pairs sleek, seductive rock with a bleak view of pleasure, technology and emotional numbness. This review hears beauty in the music, but little comfort.

sources.originalTitle: Dopamine Chamber

segments.body: Pitchfork hears Dopamine Chamber as a record about escape that refuses to offer reassurance. Its polished stadium rock draws listeners in even as Grian Chatten’s lyrics evoke compulsive pleasure, online dissociation and a society dulled by its own appetites.

segments.title: Beauty with a sting
segments.body: The review argues that the album’s glamour and pessimism depend on each other. Songs including “Marianne” and “Where Is Gone?” use alluring melodies and performances to make their darker ideas more unnerving; even the record’s portrait of romance suggests it can become another fleeting hit of pleasure.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s Danceteria becomes the duo’s final album after Dave Ball’s death
content.shortHeadline: Soft Cell’s final album is a bittersweet return to New York
content.standfirst: Marc Almond says he would not make another Soft Cell record without Dave Ball. Their completed album revisits the clubs and contradictions of early-1980s New York, now as a closing chapter.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Soft Cell had agreed that Danceteria was finished; two days later, keyboardist Dave Ball died. Singer Marc Almond calls the release their sixth and final album, saying he would not continue the group without his longtime collaborator. The record looks back to the New York club scene that shaped them after the success of “Tainted Love.”

segments.title: The city behind the songs
segments.body: Almond describes the album as a love letter to a dangerous, creative city, while also recalling the loneliness and fear he witnessed as the AIDS crisis took hold. He says the pair grew closer while making the record and feels relieved they completed it together, though saddened Ball could not see its release.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s first solo rock album carries his activist convictions
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello brings his activism to a solo rock album
content.standfirst: The Rage Against the Machine guitarist says his new record is a response to a dangerous political moment. He also recalls how his mother’s example shaped his belief in ordinary people’s power to act.

image.caption: Tom Morello.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello describes Everyone Gets What They Want as his first full-length solo rock album, built around anti-racist and anti-fascist songs. He presents it as a personal response to a global far-right resurgence and says he regards making rebellious rock as an act of resistance.

segments.title: A family inheritance
segments.body: Morello credits his mother, Mary, with instilling his politics. He recalls her taking part in civil-rights and labour causes and teaching him about the United Farm Workers’ grape boycott when he was a child. He says the belief that ordinary people can change the world runs through the music he has written.

content.headline: Spacemen 3’s The Perfect Prescription finds freedom in its rough edges
content.shortHeadline: The strange, searching pull of Spacemen 3’s The Perfect Prescription
content.standfirst: Pitchfork revisits the 1987 album as an unconventional meeting of drone, gospel feeling and guitar experiments. Its account finds the record compelling not because it perfects its ideas, but because it lets them remain ragged.

sources.originalTitle: The Perfect Prescription

segments.body: The Perfect Prescription is framed as Spacemen 3’s defining record: a guitar album that redirects attention from conventional rhythm towards repetition, texture and atmosphere. The review traces its mix of indie rock, drone, heavy psychedelia and spiritual influence, and argues that the music still sounds strange because it resists tidy resolution.

segments.title: Accident and intention
segments.body: The piece resists treating the album as a perfectly plotted trip. It describes long sessions, improvised techniques and musical ideas that sometimes emerged by chance, while also noting the record’s bleak account of drug use. Its lasting force, the reviewer suggests, lies in the tension between ecstatic sound and the loneliness beneath it.

content.headline: A Tate Britain exhibition revisits the unruly energy of 1990s culture
content.shortHeadline: The images and boundary-crossing spirit of 1990s Britain
content.standfirst: A new exhibition brings together photographs of fashion, music, clubs and street life. Its curator argues that the decade’s cultural shifts were also about who got to participate and whose voices were heard.

sources.originalTitle: 'Rock 'n' roll swagger': 10 iconic images capturing the chaotic energy of '90s Brit culture

segments.body: The BBC’s tour of Tate Britain’s The 90s: Art & Fashion moves through images of club nights, models, artists, musicians and young people out after dark. Together they evoke a decade in which music, fashion and visual art frequently crossed paths, with a restless, often contradictory energy.

segments.title: Who gets to make culture?
segments.body: Curator Edward Enninful says the period is remembered not only for its styles but for changes in who could take part and be heard. Photographers featured in the exhibition recall club scenes and informal gatherings where people made their own spaces; Enninful sees the decade’s influence as still unfolding.

content.headline: How ? and the Mysterians turned “96 Tears” into a garage-rock landmark
content.shortHeadline: The unlikely rise and long afterlife of “96 Tears”
content.standfirst: A home-recorded single by a young Mexican-American band reached the top of the US charts in 1966. Its rough-edged sound later helped shape garage rock and punk.

sources.originalTitle: 'A hypnotic effect that fills you with joy': The incredible story of 96 Tears, the US's unlikeliest one-hit wonder

segments.body: Recorded in a small Bay City studio and released by a local label, “96 Tears” became a US number one for ? and the Mysterians. The BBC traces the song from its organ riff and teen heartbreak lyrics to the band’s DIY route through local radio and, eventually, national distribution.

segments.title: A life beyond the charts
segments.body: The band did not repeat the single’s success, but the track found a second life through garage-rock revivals and later musicians who took inspiration from its raw sound. The article places the group in a regional Mexican-American music community and explains how the song’s afterlife grew well beyond its brief chart peak.

content.headline: Masterplan review: Stanley Tucci’s Louvre heist caper has a few tricks
content.shortHeadline: Masterplan’s heist tricks can’t rescue its thin story
content.standfirst: The Amazon thriller gives Stanley Tucci a chance to send up a suave criminal mastermind, but its family revelations and overextended plot keep it from making much of an impression.

image.caption: Stanley Tucci in Masterplan.

sources.originalTitle: Masterplan review – Stanley Tucci is wasted in Amazon’s smooth-brained heist caper

segments.body: In Masterplan, two young criminals are recruited by veteran thief Roger, played by Stanley Tucci, for an elaborate scheme to steal the Mona Lisa. The film offers double-crosses, gadgets and some enjoyable heist mechanics, including a clever use of a helium balloon, but its characters are too thinly drawn to give the caper much emotional weight.

The Guardian review finds Tucci game for the comedy and director Thomas Vincent effective when the film sticks to espionage. But the story’s increasingly ridiculous turns and unnecessary length leave it as forgettable streaming entertainment rather than a satisfying star vehicle.

content.headline: NAZA review: anonymous Israeli intelligence testimony casts a shadow over Gaza
content.shortHeadline: NAZA’s anonymous testimony makes for a chilling Gaza film
content.standfirst: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary presents claims by Israeli intelligence personnel about how strikes are planned. Its anonymity limits the testimony’s impact, but the film’s account is deeply unsettling.

image.caption: Tel Aviv at night, as seen in NAZA.

sources.originalTitle: NAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deaths

segments.body: NAZA uses interviews with Israeli intelligence personnel whose faces and voices are concealed. They allege that surveillance and AI-assisted systems help identify targets in Gaza, and describe projected civilian deaths as part of strike planning. These are claims made by the anonymous interviewees; the review notes that their anonymity also makes their testimony harder to assess.

segments.title: A disturbing distance
segments.body: The Guardian critic describes the film’s night-time rooftop setting in Tel Aviv as a striking contrast to the accounts of violence in Gaza. The documentary also includes testimony about military operations in northern Gaza and attacks on civilians seeking food. The review cautions against a speaker’s comparison with Nazism, while finding the film’s focus on civilian harm powerful.

content.headline: La Bola Negra connects three gay lives across a century of Spanish history
content.shortHeadline: La Bola Negra traces gay desire and history across Spain
content.standfirst: Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s film moves between 1932, 1937 and 2017, joining stories of desire, persecution and family memory. Its festival reception has fuelled awards speculation, but the film’s ambition is the stronger story.

sources.originalTitle: 'Immediately spellbinding': Four reasons why gay Spanish epic La Bola Negra could win the Oscar for best picture

segments.body: La Bola Negra follows three gay men across different periods of Spanish history: a soldier during the Civil War, a young man excluded from an elite club in 1932, and a historian in 2017. The film draws inspiration from Federico García Lorca while building its own stories around memory, sexual repression and the inheritance of family history.

segments.title: A form as expansive as its subject
segments.body: The BBC highlights the film’s shifting visual styles, its ensemble performances and its blend of historical drama, romance and family story. It reports that the film won the audience award at Toronto and has attracted awards attention; predictions about a best-picture nomination remain just that, rather than a settled outcome.

content.headline: Artificial turns OpenAI’s founding into a drama about who controls AI
content.shortHeadline: Artificial dramatises the fight over OpenAI’s future
content.standfirst: Luca Guadagnino’s film follows the growing divide between Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever. The BBC reads it as a cautionary story about AI safety and commercial power, while noting that the fictionalised characters are not equally developed.

sources.originalTitle: AI fears are growing – and unsettling new film Artificial puts them, and the future of humanity, centre stage

segments.body: Artificial traces OpenAI’s development from a nonprofit venture to the company behind ChatGPT, focusing on the conflict between co-founders Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever. The film puts questions about AI safety, secrecy and commercial interests at the centre of a story about who gets to shape the technology’s future.

segments.title: A timely but uneven warning
segments.body: The BBC says the film’s imagined scenario of AI evading a human test resonates with recent concerns raised about autonomous systems, but describes the timing as fortunate rather than prophetic. It also notes that Sutskever receives a fuller portrayal than Altman, whose motives remain less explored.

content.headline: What makes a film adaptation work? It may be the freedom to change the book
content.shortHeadline: Great film adaptations often know when to leave books behind
content.standfirst: A writer surveying adaptations from The Shining to Trainspotting argues that fidelity is no guarantee of success. The most effective films find a visual language of their own.

image.caption: A collage featuring The Shining, The Godfather and The Silence of the Lambs.

sources.originalTitle: An open book: how to make a great film adaptation, from The Shining to Trainspotting

segments.body: The essay challenges the idea that a successful film must be faithful to its source. Great novels can produce great films, and weaker books can still become effective screen stories; what matters is how a filmmaker translates the material from words into images, sound and performance.

segments.title: Adaptation as reinvention
segments.body: Examples including Children of Men, Orlando and The Shining illustrate the case for taking liberties rather than assembling a reverent list of a novel’s best-known scenes. The writer also acknowledges that there is no single version of a book in every reader’s mind, making fidelity an uncertain measure in the first place.

content.headline: Case 137 review: a police-brutality inquiry tests one officer’s loyalties
content.shortHeadline: Case 137 follows a police officer investigating police violence
content.standfirst: Dominik Moll’s procedural follows an internal-affairs officer tracing the source of a protester’s injuries. Its painstaking investigation is compelling, though the film’s conflicts do not reach the complexity it promises.

image.caption: Léa Drucker in Dossier 137.

sources.originalTitle: Case 137 review – tense gilets-jaunes thriller divides cop’s loyalties over police brutality

segments.body: In Case 137, Léa Drucker plays Stéphanie, an officer investigating injuries to a teenage protester during France’s 2018 gilets jaunes demonstrations. The inquiry turns personal when she discovers the boy is from her hometown, pushing her to pursue evidence while risking accusations that she is cutting corners herself.

The review finds the film strongest as Stéphanie and her colleagues painstakingly trace CCTV and phone footage to identify the officers involved. Its larger tensions—between police and critics, and between Paris and a left-behind provincial town—are less fully developed, but the film remains valuable in its attention to accountability.

content.headline: Ellie and Natasia bring new life experience to their sketch-show return
content.shortHeadline: Ellie and Natasia return with a changed view of their characters
content.standfirst: The comedians behind Ellie & Natasia are parents now, like some of the mothers they once spoofed. They discuss that shift, the show’s new sketches and the challenge of finding shared cultural references online.

image.caption: Natasia Demetriou and Ellie White in Ellie & Natasia.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It was like your worst nightmare’ – Ellie and Natasia on mums, music … and failing to make Bob Mortimer smile

segments.body: Ellie White and Natasia Demetriou return for a second series of their sketch show after becoming mothers themselves. They say that experience has given them a new empathy for characters such as their hygiene-obsessed mums, though they were careful not to make pregnancy the focus of the series.

segments.title: Comedy in an endless feed
segments.body: The pair have shifted away from specific musical parodies towards sketches about social-media formats, from day-in-the-life videos to visual podcasts. They say the internet makes it harder to find a shared reference everyone recognises—and sometimes a real online creator has already done the joke.

content.headline: Last One Laughing: Halloween adds screams to its no-laughing challenge
content.shortHeadline: Last One Laughing tests comedians’ poker faces with screams
content.standfirst: The Halloween special asks its comics to suppress screams as well as laughter. Its participants describe the strange pressures of the format and the careful production behind the apparent chaos.

image.caption: Daisy May Cooper on Last One Laughing: Halloween.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am’ – the spooky secrets of Last One Laughing: Halloween

segments.body: For the Halloween special of Last One Laughing, comedians must keep a straight face and avoid screaming while trying to make their competitors do either. Phil Wang says he discovered he was a screamer; host Jimmy Carr argues that jokes and jump scares draw on a similar element of surprise.

segments.title: A game built in the edit
segments.body: Contestants describe the long, exhausting hours and the effort needed to hold back two different reactions. Carr and Wang also point to the show’s challenges, props and close monitoring of every contestant; the footage, Carr says, can reveal moments even the people in the room did not notice.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans asking when it will return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain pause after its latest series
content.standfirst: The BBC’s partnership with Disney+ has ended, a planned Christmas special has been cancelled and no new Doctor has been announced. Fans and television voices disagree on what the long-running series needs next.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Since the latest series ended in 2025, Doctor Who has had no new episodes. The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+, cancelled a planned Christmas special and put future production out to tender; no new Doctor has been announced. The article reports that the BBC has declined to comment further.

segments.title: A format built to change
segments.body: The feature traces the show’s history of renewal, from its 1963 debut and 1989 cancellation to its revival in 2005. Contributors point to changing showrunners, scripts and audience responses as part of its latest troubles, while lifelong fan Frank Skinner urges the BBC to bring it back without losing sight of its established identity.

content.headline: Time’s prison drama examines how anger and isolation shape young men
content.shortHeadline: Time shows the anger and isolation inside a young offenders’ prison
content.standfirst: Jimmy McGovern’s third series moves to a young offenders’ institution, where both inmates and guards are trapped in violent hierarchies. The review links that behaviour to isolation and a weakened prison system.

image.caption: David Tennant as prison officer Bobby Bailey in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time picks up where Adolescence left off

segments.body: The third series of Time takes place in a young offenders’ institution, where boys and prison staff navigate a culture shaped by violence, fear and power. The review argues that the guards are not outside that culture: some use violence to control inmates or manage their own strained relationships.

segments.title: Anger in a system under strain
segments.body: The series connects the characters’ aggression to unmet needs for love and connection, as well as to a prison regime where isolation has replaced much of the education and training described by one officer. The review sees no easy answer in the drama, but makes a case that the conditions themselves help sustain the behaviour they punish.

content.headline: Penguin Colony turns an Antarctic expedition into a strange, searching game
content.shortHeadline: Penguin Colony is an uncanny Antarctic adventure
content.standfirst: This low-poly exploration game puts players in control of penguins gathering words as they follow an expedition into a landscape of Nazis and Lovecraftian horror. Its unsettling mix builds towards an argument against both.

image.caption: Penguin Colony, an Antarctic adventure by Origame Digital.

sources.originalTitle: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors

segments.body: Penguin Colony sends players waddling, swimming and gliding across Antarctica as they follow the trail of an expedition chasing an otherworldly presence. You can switch between penguins with different abilities; the game’s unusual collectibles are words, gathered as you explore the frozen landscape and its traces of human occupation.

segments.title: A disquieting landscape
segments.body: The review describes a world that shifts from huts and ice floes to enormous labyrinths and alien structures, layered with a scientist’s narration and disturbing scenes of Nazi collapse. It can be uneven in its controls and sound, but the critic praises its unsettling tone and conclusion, which challenges Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi brutality.

content.headline: Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake updates a classic without losing its shape
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time gets a 4K makeover on Switch 2
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s remake adds modern controls and a newly orchestrated soundtrack to the 1998 adventure. Its revised Link model may divide players, but the hands-on preview finds the game’s structure still holds up.

image.caption: Link in the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era

segments.body: The Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time gives Link a sprint, a manual jump, a movable camera and a streamlined inventory, alongside a more detailed Hyrule and newly orchestrated music. The preview finds the changes make the familiar adventure feel different under the controls while leaving its traditional dungeons and puzzles intact.

segments.title: A new look for an old world
segments.body: The preview sees Link’s glossy, doll-like appearance as the most contentious change. It raises the possibility that the design draws on Japanese puppet theatre, but notes that Nintendo has not explained its intentions. In motion, the reviewer finds the style coherent and sees no reason to conclude the game’s original identity has been ruined.

content.headline: Could independent arcades bring social gaming back to the high street?
content.shortHeadline: A new wave of arcades could make gaming social again
content.standfirst: After years of sprawling games built to hold players’ time, a columnist sees renewed interest in shorter arcade-style experiences. Small venues may offer something big publishers cannot: a local place to play together.

image.caption: A video game arcade.

sources.originalTitle: Ready player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirth

segments.body: The article argues that players are tiring of games designed to demand endless time and attention, and points to a growing interest in contained, arcade-inspired experiences. It sees an opportunity for independent venues that curate new and classic games rather than simply offering coin-ops alongside drinks.

segments.title: More than a cabinet
segments.body: Games journalist Will Freeman says that a handful of small venues are taking an approach closer to independent bookshops and record stores, including a London café focused on imported Japanese arcade machines. The appeal is not only the games, but the chance to meet other players, learn from them and build a local community.

content.headline: A £350 GTA 6 collector’s box raises questions about who can afford gaming
content.shortHeadline: The GTA 6 collector’s box puts gaming’s rising costs in view
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s merchandise box costs £350 and does not include the game. The writer sees it as part of a wider divide between accessible mobile play and premium console gaming.

image.caption: The Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI collector’s box costs £350 and contains merchandise, but not the game or a download code. Buying both the box and the listed £70 game would bring the total to £420. The writer does not object to collecting, but notes that the price is unusually high.

segments.title: A widening spending divide
segments.body: The article connects the box to rising console and game prices, arguing that premium gaming increasingly depends on disposable income. It contrasts that market with mobile games, which reach a much larger share of players at little or no cost, and worries that the kinds of expansive games the writer values are becoming harder to access.

content.headline: Japan prepares a first mission to bring samples back from a Martian moon
content.shortHeadline: Japan plans first sample-return mission to a Martian moon
content.standfirst: The five-year mission aims to collect soil from Phobos and return it to Earth, where researchers hope it can help resolve how Mars’s two small moons formed. The launch is planned for Tuesday.

image.caption: Phobos photographed by Nasa’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.

sources.originalTitle: Japan to launch world-first mission to collect samples from Martian moon

segments.body: Japan’s space agency, Jaxa, is aiming to launch the Martian Moons eXploration mission on an H3 rocket. If successful, it will be the first mission to bring samples back from Phobos, one of Mars’s two small moons. The spacecraft is expected to reach the Mars region in 2027 and return its samples to Earth in 2031.

segments.title: What researchers hope to learn
segments.body: Scientists disagree on whether Phobos and Deimos formed from debris after an impact on Mars or are captured asteroids. Jaxa hopes analysis of Phobos soil will help settle the question. The mission will also observe Deimos and collect data that may help assess the moons’ possible use in future Mars exploration.

content.headline: Warming is raising the risk of turbulence pilots cannot see
content.shortHeadline: Climate change raises the risk of invisible air turbulence
content.standfirst: Clear-air turbulence can hit at cruising altitude without showing on radar. Researchers have found it has increased over recent decades, while pilots and airlines are testing new ways to forecast and respond to the danger.

image.caption: Turbulence can injure passengers and crew when they are not secured in their seats.

sources.originalTitle: Hiding in plane sight: the invisible turbulence that can strike out of a clear blue sky

segments.body: Turbulence caused by storms is often visible on radar; clear-air turbulence is not. It commonly occurs near jet streams, where changes in wind speed or direction can jolt an aircraft. An analysis of atmospheric data from 1979 to 2020 found severe clear-air turbulence increased by 55%, with moderate and light turbulence also rising.

segments.title: Forecasts and precautions
segments.body: Researchers say warming can intensify wind shear and add energy to thunderstorms, increasing turbulence risks. Airlines share sensor reports to improve near-term forecasts, and some are exploring lidar to detect conditions ahead. The article stresses that injuries often happen when people are not buckled in; aircraft are built to withstand far more turbulence than passengers can.

content.headline: World timekeepers vote to replace leap seconds with leap hours
content.shortHeadline: Leap seconds to give way to leap hours in timekeeping change
content.standfirst: The change is intended to reduce the risk of timing errors disrupting computer systems and infrastructure. Coordinated universal time may drift by as much as an hour before a correction is needed—a prospect the report says is thousands of years away.

image.caption: A clock at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, through which the prime meridian passes.

sources.originalTitle: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour

segments.body: Delegates from 69 countries have voted to move away from leap seconds, which are added to keep official time aligned with Earth’s irregular rotation. The new approach allows coordinated universal time to drift farther from astronomical time before a correction is made, avoiding a sudden 61- or 59-second minute.

segments.title: Why the system is changing
segments.body: Atomic clocks underpin systems including communications, navigation and electricity grids, but Earth’s rotation varies. Past leap-second adjustments have caused some computer systems to freeze or go offline; a negative leap second would be untested. The report says the first leap-hour adjustment is not expected for thousands of years.

content.headline: Margaret Hamilton, Apollo software pioneer, dies aged 90
content.shortHeadline: Apollo software pioneer Margaret Hamilton dies aged 90
content.standfirst: Hamilton led the MIT team that developed software for the Apollo Guidance Computer. Her preparation helped mission controllers respond to alarms during Apollo 11’s lunar landing without aborting the mission.

image.caption: Margaret Hamilton beside a model of the Apollo command module at MIT in 1969.

sources.originalTitle: Margaret Hamilton obituary

segments.body: Margaret Hamilton directed the software engineering division at MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, which developed the computer systems used in Apollo. During Apollo 11’s descent, alarms prompted discussion of an abort. Hamilton recognised a problem she had rehearsed in simulations: a radar switch had been left active. Mission controllers reassured the crew, and the Eagle landed safely.

segments.title: A lasting contribution
segments.body: Hamilton was the first woman programmer on the Apollo project and led a team of about 100. She insisted on repeatedly testing software for faults, work the obituary says helped missions avoid known software bugs. She also coined the term “software engineering” to describe the discipline and its responsibilities.

content.headline: UK’s early flu season prompts calls for eligible people to get vaccinated
content.shortHeadline: Early flu rise prompts UK vaccination advice
content.standfirst: Flu infections remain relatively low but are rising earlier than usual, health officials say. Experts caution that an early start does not by itself mean a worse season, and explain how flu differs from common colds.

image.caption: Respiratory viruses can rise as the UK enters the colder months.

sources.originalTitle: Why so many people are sick right now

segments.body: Flu activity is rising in the UK earlier than usual, though rates remain relatively low, according to the UK Health Security Agency. Experts say the timing and severity of flu seasons vary, and an early start does not necessarily predict a worse winter. The agency is urging people eligible for an NHS flu vaccine to get it as soon as possible.

segments.title: How flu differs from a cold
segments.body: Flu usually comes on quickly, over hours, and is more likely to cause a raised temperature, fever and muscle aches. Colds more often bring a runny nose, sneezing, cough and sore throat, though symptoms can overlap. Experts say the reasons respiratory viruses peak in winter are still debated.

content.headline: Study finds high blood pressure in many UK adults under 40
content.shortHeadline: Study finds undetected high blood pressure among under-40s
content.standfirst: An analysis of a large UK study found high blood pressure in 15% of participants aged 18 to 39. Researchers say younger adults at risk may go unchecked under current NHS health-check arrangements.

image.caption: A blood-pressure check can be requested at a GP practice or pharmacy.

sources.originalTitle: The ‘silent killer’ blood pressure problem that affects under-40s too

segments.body: The study, drawing on measurements from 1.4 million UK adults, found that a third had high blood pressure; six in 10 of that group were unaware of it. Among participants aged 18 to 39, 15% had high blood pressure. The researchers caution that readings taken in a study may not reflect measurements taken at home while fully relaxed.

segments.title: How to get checked
segments.body: NHS heart-health checks are offered from age 40, but people can ask a GP or pharmacist for a blood-pressure measurement sooner. The experts quoted advise using a standard arm-cuff monitor rather than relying on phone apps or wearable devices, which they say have not generally been shown to be as accurate.

content.headline: German police detain Russian man linked to London hospital cyberattack
content.shortHeadline: Russian man detained over London hospital cyberattack
content.standfirst: The BBC says German investigators are examining whether the accused Qilin gang member was involved in the 2024 Synnovis attack, which disrupted blood testing at London hospitals. The case is also being examined for possible links to a patient’s death.

image.caption: The alleged Qilin gang member was detained by German police on arrival in Frankfurt.

sources.originalTitle: Russian man linked to deadly London hospitals hack arrested

segments.body: German police have detained a 28-year-old Russian man, identified by German media as Vladimir K., whom authorities accuse of being a core member of the Qilin cyber-crime gang. The BBC reports that German investigators have included the 2024 hack of Synnovis in their inquiry. The suspect has not been convicted.

segments.title: The impact of the attack
segments.body: The Synnovis ransomware attack disrupted pathology services at London hospitals, led to cancelled operations and diverted emergency patients, and affected more than 10,000 appointments. One hospital trust said a patient died unexpectedly after a long wait for a blood-test result, among several contributing factors. British police are examining whether their inquiry could lead to an unlawful-killing case.

content.headline: Austrian MEP urges EU action after nude deepfakes target women in politics
content.shortHeadline: MEP calls for EU action on sexualised deepfakes
content.standfirst: Lena Schilling says digitally altered nude images of her were circulated without consent. A report cited in the article found 50 MEPs had been targeted, most of them women, prompting calls to enforce an upcoming EU ban.

image.caption: Austrian MEP Lena Schilling says sexualised deepfakes of her were shared without her consent.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I felt disgusted’: MEP speaks out over nude deepfakes and urges EU action

segments.body: Austrian Green MEP Lena Schilling says she felt disgusted after finding nude deepfakes made from images of her at a press conference. A report by the Berlin-based thinktank Agora Digitale Transformation says 50 MEPs—46 women—have been targeted by sexualised deepfakes. Schilling calls the images digital violence and says they can discourage women from entering public life.

segments.title: A ban and questions about enforcement
segments.body: Schilling and German Green MEP Terry Reintke led a letter signed by 119 MEPs urging the EU to pair a ban on AI undressing apps and websites, scheduled to take effect on 2 December, with effective enforcement. Schilling says rules “on paper” will not protect people if loopholes allow the tools to keep operating.

content.headline: Rural Norfolk data-centre plan would use up to a gigawatt of power
content.shortHeadline: Norfolk data-centre plan raises power and land concerns
content.standfirst: A developer’s proposal near Tilney St Lawrence includes a data centre and solar farms across about 4,695 acres. Residents and local officials have raised concerns about water, construction traffic, nature and the site’s proximity to RAF Marham.

image.caption: Resident Sophie Pendrick says the proposed data-centre project has left her shocked by its scale.

sources.originalTitle: How has community reacted to major data centre plan?

segments.body: Evolution Power Limited proposes a data centre near Tilney St Lawrence in Fenland, Norfolk, with a maximum demand of one gigawatt of power. The plan also includes solar farms with a combined area of about 4,695 acres and up to 1.3 gigawatts of generating capacity. The developer says the project would support digital services and create jobs.

segments.title: Local concerns and next steps
segments.body: Residents have questioned the project’s scale, water use and construction traffic. The local council leader also raised concerns about nearby nature sites, roads and whether solar panels could affect RAF Marham. Because the proposal is classed as a nationally significant infrastructure project, the final decision rests with government; a public consultation is open until 26 November.

content.headline: Electronic noses help cities trace the source of industrial odours
content.shortHeadline: Cities use sensors to trace industrial odours
content.standfirst: Air monitors paired with weather data are helping officials identify which facilities may be responsible when bad smells prompt complaints. The approach offers evidence where odour rules are limited, though smell remains subjective.

image.caption: Newby Island landfill operators have been ordered to track odours with monitors and drones.

sources.originalTitle: Living with a stink? Technology might help

segments.body: In Des Moines, Iowa, a ring of monitors measures chemical compounds in the air alongside local weather conditions. Officials say the combined data can help trace an odour plume to a facility, replacing the earlier practice of driving to a complaint and sniffing the air. The city spends about $240,000 a year on the monitoring system.

segments.title: Monitoring is not the same as removing the smell
segments.body: In Milpitas, California, landfill operators have been ordered to use drones and install monitors to track odour-causing chemicals. Treatment can absorb, chemically change or burn away target compounds, but experts say it can be expensive; some cheaper masking sprays are viewed sceptically. Even with better evidence, people’s sensitivity to smells differs.

content.headline: Anthropic researchers warn of self-replicating AI worms, but experts differ on U
content.shortHeadline: AI worm warning draws both concern and scepticism
content.standfirst: Anthropic researchers say a test program spread across internet-connected televisions by splitting its workload. They warn future systems could adapt to more devices, while other security experts say the demonstrated worm was slow and not yet a major practical threat.

sources.originalTitle: What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?

segments.body: Anthropic’s offensive research team says it built a malicious AI program that spread through internet-connected televisions, dividing parts of itself among 15 devices. The researchers warn that a more capable program able to run on less powerful hardware could become feasible by the end of the year. The report describes a test, not a widespread outbreak.

segments.title: How serious is the threat?
segments.body: Some experts say AI could help malicious software adapt to new vulnerabilities, and that poorly maintained smart devices can be hard to secure. Others quoted in the report argue the demonstrated program moved slowly, that worms can be detected and blocked, and that strong passwords and two-factor authentication would stop many attacks. Experts do not agree on how high this risk should rank.

content.headline: World Bank backs small AI models for low-connectivity communities
content.shortHeadline: World Bank promotes small AI built for local needs
content.standfirst: The bank says specialised models that run on phones and work in local languages could help meet needs such as farmers’ access to soil advice. That promise depends on basic infrastructure and should be weighed against concerns about jobs and unequal access.

image.caption: Small AI models designed for phones could work in places with limited connectivity.

sources.originalTitle: World Bank says ‘small AI’ could transform developing countries

segments.body: The World Bank is urging governments and partners to develop “small AI” models designed for specific tasks, local languages and limited connectivity. Its chief knowledge officer cited Indian farmers who could use a phone-based tool to access soil analysis—support that cannot readily be provided by human specialists to every small farm.

segments.title: The infrastructure gap
segments.body: The IMF’s managing director said broad access to AI depends on electricity, digital infrastructure and safeguards. The report notes that many rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa lack electricity or consistent internet access, while the IMF also warned that AI could change or eliminate a substantial share of jobs worldwide, with young people particularly exposed.

content.headline: AI agents face blocks as websites tighten access to online services
content.shortHeadline: Websites block AI agents over security and business concerns
content.standfirst: Companies including airlines, banks and retailers are restricting automated agents, complicating tech firms’ promises that AI can handle online tasks for users. Security controls, data licensing and the value of human visits are all part of the dispute.

sources.originalTitle: Websites are closing their doors to AI agents

segments.body: AI companies are promoting agents that can book, shop and manage online tasks, but many websites restrict their access. The report says Delta blocks agents from booking tickets, while JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have confirmed they block agents from accounts over security concerns. Yelp allows access only through its paid data-licensing programme.

segments.title: A less open web?
segments.body: Some businesses say agents should act on behalf of customers; others object to automated access or the loss of human visits and advertising exposure. Anti-bot safeguards can also block legitimate agents. The result may be more checks for people using websites, even when companies’ systems were designed to catch bots rather than AI assistants.

content.headline: Anthropic says AI use is reshaping its hiring and daily work
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic reports fewer junior hires and more meetings
